hallmark: no wings at all, and the waist between the alitrunk and the gaster that is left as a gap

reference.title: Ants, Bees, and Wasps, plate 2 figure 5

doc: *Formica rufa*, dorsal — the red wood ant, worker.
Traced from figure 5 of plate 2 of John Lubbock's *Ants, Bees, and Wasps*,
where the plate's own caption names it and the other four figures are *Atta*
and *Pheidole*. `references/formica-rufa.jpg` is the plate; the wood ant is
the large figure at the bottom, drawn square to the page with all six legs
and both antennae clear of the body.
## The first plate with no wings
Which is why `REQUIRED_PARTS.hymenoptera` no longer asks for any. A worker
ant has none — not folded, not reduced, none — and neither do the females of
a good many other families in the order, so the list was asking for a part
that is optional rather than for one whose absence is a mistake. The
bumblebee's and the hornet's own tests assert their four wings, which is
where a fact about one species belongs.
`morphology.wingCover` says `absent`, and this is the only record in the
collection that does. It is worth a plate on its own account for that: the
key's first question is what covers the back, and until this animal arrived
one of its six answers led nowhere.
## What the drawing has to get right
The **waist**. An ant is three parts with two constrictions, and the
constrictions are the order: head, alitrunk, gaster, with the petiole
between the last two. Drawn as a *gap* — the alitrunk ends at y = 568 and
the gaster starts at 582 — on the same reasoning the bumblebee's plate uses,
which is that a waist is the absence of an animal rather than a part of one.
Then the **antennae**, which are elbowed. A long scape from the head, a bend,
and the funiculus carrying on at an angle: `geniculate` is the character
state and `ANTENNA_FORMS` has no such word, so the record says `filiform`,
which is the closest true thing — the joints past the elbow are a chain of
equal segments. The drawing says the rest.
Then the **head**, which is nearly square with a slightly notched back
margin, and as wide as the gaster. A worker's head carries the mandibles and
the muscle to close them, and the notch at the occiput is where a
*Formica*'s neck sits.
## Plate space
y = 0 at the front of the head, y = 1000 at the tip of the gaster. Head 0 to
238, alitrunk 248 to 568, gaster 578 to 1004. The antennae reach x = 444 and
above y = -84; the hind tarsi reach y = 1090.

note: The legs first, so they pass under the body.
Long and fine — a wood ant walks fifty metres from its nest and back — and
much finer than any beetle's here: the femur is 26 units against the
violet ground beetle's 34 on an animal a third of the length. The spines
Lubbock draws on each tibia are left out; at eighty pixels they are a
furred outline.
The gaster — the ant's abdomen behind the waist. Broad, smooth and
shining, and where a wood ant carries the formic acid it sprays.
The tergite lines across the gaster: three strokes, each crossing the
axis. Both guides are centred on x = 0, which is the case the fan
validator allows on the midline.
The pubescence on the gaster, as five strokes. A wood ant is not furred
the way a bumblebee is, but it is not bare either, and hatching is what
an engraving has for the difference.
The alitrunk: the middle section, which in a wingless worker is the
thorax with nothing on it. Its profile from above steps in twice — the
pronotum, then the mesonotum, then the propodeum — and those steps are
the only structure this part of the animal has.
It stops at y = 568 and the gaster starts at 578. The ten units between
them are the petiole, and they are drawn as nothing at all: a waist is
the absence of an animal rather than a part of one, and the bumblebee's
plate makes the same call for the same reason.
The head: nearly square, as wide as the gaster, with the back margin
slightly notched where the neck sits. A worker's head is mostly the
muscle that closes its mandibles.
A mandible: triangular and toothed on the animal, drawn open here.
Crossed in front of the head as an ant usually carries them, two of them
at plate size are one blot.
The three ocelli on the vertex, in a small triangle between the compound
eyes: one on the midline, drawn once, and a pair either side of it. A
wood ant worker has them and most smaller ants do not, so they are worth
the three parts.
The sculpture on the head, as three strokes. A Formica's head is finely
striate rather than smooth, which is the difference between it and the
polished gaster below.
The antenna, elbowed. One long scape out of the head, a bend, and four
funicular joints carrying on at an angle — which is what an ant's antenna
does and what no other antenna in this collection does.
`ANTENNA_FORMS` has no `geniculate`, so the record answers `filiform`:
true of the joints past the elbow, and the closest of six wrong answers
to the whole. The bend is drawn rather than recorded.
